examples.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
examples.problem: Given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069543/assets/93c4cdd7a16be0f08bd161b97dde5002a3f12dee2febd3857fe9da289f9a9c4a.png) and $A^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
examples.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+54 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}+A-2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}+A-2I) & =O \\ A+I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}I\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{1}{2},$ $q=\dfrac{1}{2},$ and 

$$
p+q=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=1.
$$

feedback.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\text{tr}(A)=-14$ and $\text{det}(A)=25.$ Then, ${A}^{2}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-14A-25I.\end{aligned}
$$
